segs.e: Linked Discourses 17.1
Chapter One
Grim
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṁ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,
“Mendicants!”
“Venerable sir,” they replied.
The Buddha said this:

segs.p: “Dāruṇo, bhikkhave, lābhasakkārasiloko kaṭuko pharuso antarāyiko anuttarassa yogakkhemassa adhigamāya.
segs.e: “Possessions, honor, and popularity are grim, bitter, and harsh. They’re an obstacle to reaching the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.
So you should train like this:

segs.p: ‘uppannaṁ lābhasakkārasilokaṁ pajahissāma, na ca no uppanno lābhasakkārasiloko cittaṁ pariyādāya ṭhassatī’ti.
segs.e: ‘We will give up arisen possessions, honor, and popularity, and we won’t let them occupy our minds.’
That’s how you should train.”
Linked Discourses 17.2
Chapter One
A Hook
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: “Dāruṇo, bhikkhave, lābhasakkārasiloko kaṭuko pharuso antarāyiko anuttarassa yogakkhemassa adhigamāya.
segs.e: “Possessions, honor, and popularity are grim, bitter, and harsh. They’re an obstacle to reaching the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, bāḷisiko āmisagataṁ baḷisaṁ gambhīre udakarahade pakkhipeyya.
segs.e: Suppose an angler was to cast a baited hook into a deep lake.
Seeing the bait, a fish would swallow it.

segs.p: Evañhi so, bhikkhave, maccho gilabaḷiso bāḷisikassa anayaṁ āpanno byasanaṁ āpanno yathākāmakaraṇīyo bāḷisikassa.
segs.e: And so the fish that swallowed the hook would meet with tragedy and disaster, and the angler can do what he wants with it.

segs.p: Bāḷisikoti kho, bhikkhave, mārassetaṁ pāpimato adhivacanaṁ.
segs.e: ‘Angler’ is a term for Māra the Wicked.
‘Hook’ is a term for possessions, honor, and popularity.

segs.p: Yo hi koci, bhikkhave, bhikkhu uppannaṁ lābhasakkārasilokaṁ assādeti nikāmeti, ayaṁ vuccati, bhikkhave, bhikkhu gilabaḷiso mārassa anayaṁ āpanno byasanaṁ āpanno yathākāmakaraṇīyo pāpimato.
segs.e: Whoever enjoys and likes arisen possessions, honor, and popularity is called a mendicant who has swallowed Māra’s hook. They’ve met with tragedy and disaster, and the Wicked One can do with them what he wants.

segs.p: Evaṁ dāruṇo kho, bhikkhave, lābhasakkārasiloko kaṭuko pharuso antarāyiko anuttarassa yogakkhemassa adhigamāya.
segs.e: So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity—bitter and harsh, an obstacle to reaching the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.
So you should train like this:

segs.p: ‘uppannaṁ lābhasakkārasilokaṁ pajahissāma, na ca no uppanno lābhasakkārasiloko cittaṁ pariyādāya ṭhassatī’ti.
segs.e: ‘We will give up arisen possessions, honor, and popularity, and we won’t let them occupy our minds.’
That’s how you should train.”
Linked Discourses 17.3
Chapter One
A Turtle
At Sāvatthī.
“Possessions, honor, and popularity are grim …

segs.p: Bhūtapubbaṁ, bhikkhave, aññatarasmiṁ udakarahade mahākummakulaṁ ciranivāsi ahosi.
segs.e: Once upon a time, in a certain lake there was a large family of turtles that had lived there for a long time.

segs.p: Atha kho, bhikkhave, aññataro kummo aññataraṁ kummaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then one of the turtles said to another,

segs.p: ‘mā kho tvaṁ, tāta kumma, etaṁ padesaṁ agamāsī’ti.
segs.e: ‘My dear turtle, don’t you go to that place.’

segs.p: Agamāsi kho, bhikkhave, so kummo taṁ padesaṁ.
segs.e: But that turtle did go to that place,
and a hunter pierced her with a harpoon.

segs.p: Atha kho, bhikkhave, so kummo yena so kummo tenupasaṅkami.
segs.e: Then that turtle went back to the other turtle.

segs.p: Addasā kho, bhikkhave, so kummo taṁ kummaṁ dūratova āgacchantaṁ.
segs.e: When the other turtle saw her coming off in the distance,
he said,

segs.p: ‘kacci tvaṁ, tāta kumma, na taṁ padesaṁ agamāsī’ti?
segs.e: ‘My dear turtle, I hope you didn’t go to that place!’
‘I did.’
‘But my dear turtle, I hope you’re not hurt or injured!’

segs.p: ‘Akkhato khomhi, tāta kumma, anupahato, atthi ca me idaṁ suttakaṁ piṭṭhito piṭṭhito anubandhan’ti.
segs.e: ‘I’m not hurt or injured. But this cord keeps dragging behind me.’
‘Indeed, my dear turtle, you’re hurt and injured!

segs.p: Etena hi te, tāta kumma, suttakena pitaro ca pitāmahā ca anayaṁ āpannā byasanaṁ āpannā.
segs.e: Your father and grandfather met with tragedy and disaster because of such a cord.

segs.p: Gaccha dāni tvaṁ, tāta kumma, na dāni tvaṁ amhākan’ti.
segs.e: Go now, you are no longer one of us.’

segs.p: Luddoti kho, bhikkhave, mārassetaṁ pāpimato adhivacanaṁ.
segs.e: ‘Hunter’ is a term for Māra the Wicked.
‘Harpoon’ is a term for possessions, honor, and popularity.
‘Cord’ is a term for greed and relishing.

segs.p: Yo hi koci, bhikkhave, bhikkhu uppannaṁ lābhasakkārasilokaṁ assādeti nikāmeti—
segs.e: Whoever enjoys and likes arisen possessions, honor, and popularity is called a mendicant who has been pierced with a harpoon. They’ve met with tragedy and disaster, and the Wicked One can do with them what he wants.

segs.p: ayaṁ vuccati, bhikkhave, bhikkhu giddho papatāya anayaṁ āpanno byasanaṁ āpanno yathākāmakaraṇīyo pāpimato.

segs.e: So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”
Linked Discourses 17.4
Chapter One
A Fleecy Sheep
At Sāvatthī.
“Possessions, honor, and popularity are grim …

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, dīghalomikā eḷakā kaṇṭakagahanaṁ paviseyya.
segs.e: Suppose a fleecy sheep was to enter a briar patch.

segs.p: Sā tatra tatra sajjeyya, tatra tatra gayheyya, tatra tatra bajjheyya, tatra tatra anayabyasanaṁ āpajjeyya.
segs.e: She’d get caught, snagged, and trapped at every turn, coming to ruin.

segs.p: Evameva kho, bhikkhave, idhekacco bhikkhu lābhasakkārasilokena abhibhūto pariyādiṇṇacitto pubbaṇhasamayaṁ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya gāmaṁ vā nigamaṁ vā piṇḍāya pavisati.
segs.e: In the same way, take a certain mendicant whose mind is overcome and overwhelmed by possessions, honor, and popularity. They robe up in the morning and, taking their bowl and robe, enter the village or town for alms.

segs.p: So tatra tatra sajjati, tatra tatra gayhati, tatra tatra bajjhati, tatra tatra anayabyasanaṁ āpajjati.
segs.e: They get caught, snagged, and trapped at every turn, coming to ruin.
So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”
Linked Discourses 17.5
Chapter One
A Dung Beetle
At Sāvatthī.
“Possessions, honor, and popularity are grim …

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, mīḷhakā gūthādī gūthapūrā puṇṇā gūthassa. Purato cassa mahāgūthapuñjo.
segs.e: Suppose there was a dung-eating beetle full of dung, stuffed with dung, and before her was a big pile of dung.
She’d look down on other beetles, thinking:

segs.p: ‘ahamhi gūthādī gūthapūrā puṇṇā gūthassa, purato ca myāyaṁ mahāgūthapuñjo’ti.
segs.e: ‘For I am a dung-eating beetle full of dung, stuffed with dung, and before me is a big pile of dung.’

segs.p: Evameva kho, bhikkhave, idhekacco bhikkhu lābhasakkārasilokena abhibhūto pariyādiṇṇacitto pubbaṇhasamayaṁ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya gāmaṁ vā nigamaṁ vā piṇḍāya pavisati.
segs.e: In the same way, take a certain mendicant whose mind is overcome and overwhelmed by possessions, honor, and popularity. They robe up in the morning and, taking their bowl and robe, enter the village or town for alms.

segs.p: So tattha bhuttāvī ca hoti yāvadattho, nimantito ca svātanāya, piṇḍapāto cassa pūro.
segs.e: There they eat as much as they like, get invited back tomorrow, and have plenty of almsfood.

segs.p: So ārāmaṁ gantvā bhikkhugaṇassa majjhe vikatthati:
segs.e: When they get back to the monastery, they boast in the middle of a group of mendicants:

segs.p: ‘bhuttāvī camhi yāvadattho, nimantito camhi svātanāya, piṇḍapāto ca myāyaṁ pūro, lābhī camhi cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānappaccayabhesajjaparikkhārānaṁ, ime panaññe bhikkhū appapuññā appesakkhā na lābhino cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānappaccayabhesajjaparikkhārānan’ti.
segs.e: ‘I ate as much as I liked, got invited back tomorrow, and had plenty of almsfood. I get robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick. But these other mendicants have little merit or significance, so they don’t get these things.’

segs.p: So tena lābhasakkārasilokena abhibhūto pariyādiṇṇacitto aññe pesale bhikkhū atimaññati.
segs.e: With a mind overcome and overwhelmed by possessions, honor, and popularity, they look down on other good-hearted mendicants.

segs.p: Tañhi tassa, bhikkhave, moghapurisassa hoti dīgharattaṁ ahitāya dukkhāya.
segs.e: This will be for their lasting harm and suffering.
So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”
Linked Discourses 17.6
Chapter One
A Bolt of Lightning
At Sāvatthī.
“Possessions, honor, and popularity are grim …

segs.p: Kaṁ, bhikkhave, asanivicakkaṁ āgacchatu, sekhaṁ appattamānasaṁ lābhasakkārasiloko anupāpuṇātu.
segs.e: Let forked lightning fall on whom? Let possessions, honor, and popularity come to a trainee who has not achieved their heart’s desire.
‘Forked lightning’ is a term for possessions, honor, and popularity.
So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”
Linked Discourses 17.7
Chapter One
A Poisoned Arrow
At Sāvatthī.
“Possessions, honor, and popularity are grim …

segs.p: Kaṁ, bhikkhave, diddhagatena visallena sallena vijjhatu, sekhaṁ appattamānasaṁ lābhasakkārasiloko anupāpuṇātu.
segs.e: Let whom be pierced by a poisoned arrow? Let possessions, honor, and popularity come to a trainee who has not achieved their heart’s desire.
‘Arrow’ is a term for possessions, honor, and popularity.
So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”
Linked Discourses 17.8
Chapter One
A Jackal
At Sāvatthī.
“Possessions, honor, and popularity are grim …

segs.p: Assuttha no tumhe, bhikkhave, rattiyā paccūsasamayaṁ jarasiṅgālassa vassamānassā”ti?
segs.e: Mendicants, did you hear an old jackal howling at the crack of dawn?”
“Yes, sir.”

segs.p: “Eso kho, bhikkhave, jarasiṅgālo ukkaṇḍakena nāma rogajātena phuṭṭho neva bilagato ramati, na rukkhamūlagato ramati, na ajjhokāsagato ramati;
segs.e: “That old jackal has the disease called mange. He’s not happy in his den, or at the root of a tree, or out in the open.

segs.p: yena yena gacchati, yattha yattha tiṭṭhati, yattha yattha nisīdati, yattha yattha nipajjati; tattha tattha anayabyasanaṁ āpajjati.
segs.e: Wherever he goes, stands, sits, or lies down he meets with tragedy and disaster.

segs.p: Evameva kho, bhikkhave, idhekacco bhikkhu lābhasakkārasilokena abhibhūto pariyādiṇṇacitto neva suññāgāragato ramati, na rukkhamūlagato ramati, na ajjhokāsagato ramati;
segs.e: In the same way, take a certain mendicant whose mind is overcome and overwhelmed by possessions, honor, and popularity. They’re not happy in an empty hut, at the root of a tree, or out in the open.

segs.p: yena yena gacchati, yattha yattha tiṭṭhati, yattha yattha nisīdati, yattha yattha nipajjati; tattha tattha anayabyasanaṁ āpajjati.
segs.e: Wherever they go, stand, sit, or lie down they meet with tragedy and disaster.
So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”
Linked Discourses 17.9
Chapter One
Gale-force Winds
At Sāvatthī.
“Possessions, honor, and popularity are grim …

segs.p: Upari, bhikkhave, ākāse verambhā nāma vātā vāyanti.
segs.e: High in the atmosphere there are gale-force winds blowing.

segs.p: Tattha yo pakkhī gacchati tamenaṁ verambhā vātā khipanti.
segs.e: Any bird that flies there is flung about by those gale-force winds.

segs.p: Tassa verambhavātakkhittassa aññeneva pādā gacchanti, aññena pakkhā gacchanti, aññena sīsaṁ gacchati, aññena kāyo gacchati.
segs.e: Their feet go one way, their wings another, their head another, and their body another.

segs.p: Evameva kho, bhikkhave, idhekacco bhikkhu lābhasakkārasilokena abhibhūto pariyādiṇṇacitto pubbaṇhasamayaṁ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya gāmaṁ vā nigamaṁ vā piṇḍāya pavisati arakkhiteneva kāyena arakkhitāya vācāya arakkhitena cittena, anupaṭṭhitāya satiyā, asaṁvutehi indriyehi.
segs.e: In the same way, take a certain monk whose mind is overcome and overwhelmed by possessions, honor, and popularity. He robes up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, enters the village or town for alms without guarding body, speech, and mind, without establishing mindfulness, and without restraining the sense faculties.

segs.p: So tattha passati mātugāmaṁ dunnivatthaṁ vā duppārutaṁ vā.
segs.e: There he sees a lady scantily clad, with revealing clothes.

segs.p: Tassa mātugāmaṁ disvā dunnivatthaṁ vā duppārutaṁ vā rāgo cittaṁ anuddhaṁseti.
segs.e: Lust infects his mind.

segs.p: So rāgānuddhaṁsitena cittena sikkhaṁ paccakkhāya hīnāyāvattati.
segs.e: He resigns the training and returns to a lesser life.

segs.p: Tassa aññe cīvaraṁ haranti, aññe pattaṁ haranti, aññe nisīdanaṁ haranti, aññe sūcigharaṁ haranti, verambhavātakkhittasseva sakuṇassa.
segs.e: Some take his robe, others his bowl, others his sitting cloth, others his needle case, just like the bird flung about by the gale-force winds.
So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”
Linked Discourses 17.10
Chapter One
With Verses
At Sāvatthī.
“Possessions, honor, and popularity are grim …

segs.p: Idhāhaṁ, bhikkhave, ekaccaṁ puggalaṁ passāmi sakkārena abhibhūtaṁ pariyādiṇṇacittaṁ, kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā apāyaṁ duggatiṁ vinipātaṁ nirayaṁ upapannaṁ.
segs.e: Take a case where I see a certain individual whose mind is overcome and overwhelmed by honor. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

segs.p: Idha panāhaṁ, bhikkhave, ekaccaṁ puggalaṁ passāmi asakkārena abhibhūtaṁ pariyādiṇṇacittaṁ, kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā apāyaṁ duggatiṁ vinipātaṁ nirayaṁ upapannaṁ.
segs.e: Take another case where I see a certain individual whose mind is overcome and overwhelmed by lack of honor. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

segs.p: Idha panāhaṁ, bhikkhave, ekaccaṁ puggalaṁ passāmi sakkārena ca asakkārena ca tadubhayena abhibhūtaṁ pariyādiṇṇacittaṁ, kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā apāyaṁ duggatiṁ vinipātaṁ nirayaṁ upapannaṁ.
segs.e: And take another case where I see a certain individual whose mind is overcome and overwhelmed by both honor and lack of honor. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.
So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”
That is what the Buddha said.

segs.p: Idaṁ vatvāna sugato athāparaṁ etadavoca satthā:
segs.e: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:
“Whether they’re honored
or not honored, or both,
their immersion doesn’t waver
as they abide in the immeasurables.
They persistently meditate
with subtle view and discernment.
Rejoicing in the ending of grasping,
they’re said to be a true person.”
Linked Discourses 17.11
Chapter Two
A Gold Cup
At Sāvatthī.
“Possessions, honor, and popularity are grim …

segs.p: Idhāhaṁ, bhikkhave, ekaccaṁ puggalaṁ evaṁ cetasā ceto paricca pajānāmi:
segs.e: When I’ve comprehended the mind of a certain individual, I understand:

segs.p: ‘na cāyamāyasmā suvaṇṇapātiyāpi rūpiyacuṇṇaparipūrāya hetu sampajānamusā bhāseyyā’ti.
segs.e: ‘This venerable would not tell a deliberate lie even for the sake of a gold cup filled with silver powder.’

segs.p: Tamenaṁ passāmi aparena samayena lābhasakkārasilokena abhibhūtaṁ pariyādiṇṇacittaṁ sampajānamusā bhāsantaṁ.
segs.e: But some time later I see them tell a deliberate lie because their mind is overcome and overwhelmed by possessions, honor, and popularity.
So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”
Linked Discourses 17.12
Chapter Two
A Silver Pot
At Sāvatthī.
“Possessions, honor, and popularity are grim …

segs.p: idhāhaṁ, bhikkhave, ekaccaṁ puggalaṁ evaṁ cetasā ceto paricca pajānāmi:
segs.e: When I’ve comprehended the mind of a certain individual, I understand:

segs.p: ‘na cāyamāyasmā rūpiyapātiyāpi suvaṇṇacuṇṇaparipūrāya hetu sampajānamusā bhāseyyā’ti.
segs.e: ‘This venerable would not tell a deliberate lie even for the sake of a silver cup filled with gold powder.’

segs.p: Tamenaṁ passāmi aparena samayena lābhasakkārasilokena abhibhūtaṁ pariyādiṇṇacittaṁ sampajānamusā bhāsantaṁ.
segs.e: But some time later I see them tell a deliberate lie because their mind is overcome and overwhelmed by possessions, honor, and popularity.
So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”
Linked Discourses 17.13–20
Chapter Two
A Gold Ingot, Etc.
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: “Idhāhaṁ, bhikkhave, ekaccaṁ puggalaṁ evaṁ cetasā ceto paricca pajānāmi:
segs.e: “Mendicants, when I’ve comprehended the mind of a certain individual, I understand:
‘This venerable would not tell a deliberate lie even for the sake of a gold ingot.’ …”
“‘… for the sake of a hundred gold ingots.’ …”
“‘… for the sake of a mountain of gold.’ …”
“‘… for the sake of a hundred mountains of gold.’ …”
“‘… for the sake of the whole earth full of gold.’ …”
“‘… for any kind of material reward.’ …”
“‘… for the sake of life.’ …”
“‘… for the sake of the finest lady in the land.’

segs.p: Tamenaṁ passāmi aparena samayena lābhasakkārasilokena abhibhūtaṁ pariyādiṇṇacittaṁ sampajānamusā bhāsantaṁ.
segs.e: But some time later I see them tell a deliberate lie because their mind is overcome and overwhelmed by possessions, honor, and popularity.
So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”
Linked Discourses 17.21
Chapter Three
A Lady
At Sāvatthī.
“Possessions, honor, and popularity are grim …

segs.p: na tassa, bhikkhave, mātugāmo eko ekassa cittaṁ pariyādāya tiṭṭhati yassa lābhasakkārasiloko cittaṁ pariyādāya tiṭṭhati.
segs.e: Even if you’re alone with a lady she might not occupy your mind, but possessions, honor and popularity would still occupy your mind.
So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”
Linked Discourses 17.22
Chapter Three
The Finest Lady in the Land
At Sāvatthī.
“Possessions, honor, and popularity are grim …

segs.p: na tassa, bhikkhave, janapadakalyāṇī ekā ekassa cittaṁ pariyādāya tiṭṭhati yassa lābhasakkārasiloko cittaṁ pariyādāya tiṭṭhati.
segs.e: Even if you’re alone with the finest lady in the land she might not occupy your mind, but possessions, honor and popularity would still occupy your mind.
So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”
Linked Discourses 17.23
Chapter Three
An Only Son
At Sāvatthī.
“Possessions, honor, and popularity are grim …

segs.p: saddhā, bhikkhave, upāsikā ekaputtakaṁ piyaṁ manāpaṁ evaṁ sammā āyācamānā āyāceyya:
segs.e: A faithful laywoman with a dear and beloved only son would rightly appeal to him,

segs.p: ‘tādiso, tāta, bhavāhi yādiso citto ca gahapati hatthako ca āḷavako’ti.
segs.e: ‘My darling, please be like the householder Citta and Hatthaka of Āḷavī.’

segs.p: Esā, bhikkhave, tulā etaṁ pamāṇaṁ mama sāvakānaṁ upāsakānaṁ, yadidaṁ citto ca gahapati hatthako ca āḷavako.
segs.e: These are a standard and a measure for my male lay disciples, that is, the householder Citta and Hatthaka of Āḷavī.

segs.p: Sace kho tvaṁ, tāta, agārasmā anagāriyaṁ pabbajasi;
segs.e: ‘But my darling, if you go forth from the lay life to homelessness,
please be like Sāriputta and Moggallāna.’

segs.p: Esā, bhikkhave, tulā etaṁ pamāṇaṁ mama sāvakānaṁ bhikkhūnaṁ, yadidaṁ sāriputtamoggalānā.
segs.e: These are a standard and a measure for my monk disciples, that is, Sāriputta and Moggallāna.

segs.p: Mā ca kho tvaṁ, tāta, sekhaṁ appattamānasaṁ lābhasakkārasiloko anupāpuṇātūti.
segs.e: ‘And my darling, may you not come into possessions, honor, and popularity while you’re still a trainee and haven’t achieved your heart’s desire.’

segs.p: Tañce, bhikkhave, bhikkhuṁ sekhaṁ appattamānasaṁ lābhasakkārasiloko anupāpuṇāti, so tassa hoti antarāyāya.
segs.e: If a trainee who hasn’t achieved their heart’s desire comes into possessions, honor, and popularity it’s an obstacle for them.
So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”
Linked Discourses 17.24
Chapter Three
An Only Daughter
At Sāvatthī.
“Possessions, honor, and popularity are grim …

segs.p: saddhā bhikkhave upāsikā ekaṁ dhītaraṁ piyaṁ manāpaṁ evaṁ sammā āyācamānā āyāceyya:
segs.e: A faithful laywoman with a dear and beloved only daughter would rightly appeal to her,

segs.p: ‘tādisā, ayye, bhavāhi yādisā khujjuttarā ca upāsikā veḷukaṇḍakiyā ca nandamātā’ti.
segs.e: ‘My darling, please be like the laywomen Khujjuttarā and Veḷukaṇṭakī, Nanda’s mother.’

segs.p: Esā, bhikkhave, tulā etaṁ pamāṇaṁ mama sāvikānaṁ upāsikānaṁ, yadidaṁ khujjuttarā ca upāsikā veḷukaṇḍakiyā ca nandamātā.
segs.e: These are a standard and a measure for my female lay disciples, that is, the laywomen Khujjuttarā and Veḷukaṇṭakī, Nanda’s mother.

segs.p: Sace kho tvaṁ, ayye, agārasmā anagāriyaṁ pabbajasi;
segs.e: ‘But my darling, if you go forth from the lay life to homelessness,

segs.p: tādisā, ayye, bhavāhi yādisā khemā ca bhikkhunī uppalavaṇṇā cāti.
segs.e: please be like the nuns Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā.’

segs.p: Esā, bhikkhave, tulā etaṁ pamāṇaṁ mama sāvikānaṁ bhikkhunīnaṁ, yadidaṁ khemā ca bhikkhunī uppalavaṇṇā ca.
segs.e: These are a standard and a measure for my nun disciples, that is, the nuns Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā.

segs.p: Mā ca kho tvaṁ, ayye, sekhaṁ appattamānasaṁ lābhasakkārasiloko anupāpuṇātūti.
segs.e: ‘And my darling, may you not come into possessions, honor, and popularity while you’re still a trainee and haven’t achieved your heart’s desire.’

segs.p: Tañce, bhikkhave, bhikkhuniṁ sekhaṁ appattamānasaṁ lābhasakkārasiloko anupāpuṇāti, so tassā hoti antarāyāya.
segs.e: If a trainee who hasn’t achieved their heart’s desire comes into possessions, honor, and popularity it’s an obstacle for them.
So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”
Linked Discourses 17.25
Chapter Three
Ascetics and Brahmins
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: “Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā lābhasakkārasilokassa assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṁ nappajānanti,
segs.e: “Mendicants, there are ascetics and brahmins who don’t truly understand the gratification, drawback, and escape when it comes to possessions, honor, and popularity.

segs.p: na me te, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā samaṇesu vā samaṇasammatā brāhmaṇesu vā brāhmaṇasammatā, na ca pana te āyasmantā sāmaññatthaṁ vā brahmaññatthaṁ vā diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṁ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharanti.
segs.e: I don’t deem them as true ascetics and brahmins. Those venerables don’t realize the goal of life as an ascetic or brahmin, and don’t live having realized it with their own insight in this very life.

segs.p: Ye ca kho keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā lābhasakkārasilokassa assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṁ pajānanti,
segs.e: There are ascetics and brahmins who do truly understand the gratification, drawback, and escape when it comes to possessions, honor, and popularity.

segs.p: te ca kho me, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā samaṇesu ceva samaṇasammatā brāhmaṇesu ca brāhmaṇasammatā, te ca panāyasmanto sāmaññatthañca brahmaññatthañca diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṁ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharantī”ti.
segs.e: I deem them as true ascetics and brahmins. Those venerables realize the goal of life as an ascetic or brahmin, and live having realized it with their own insight.”
Linked Discourses 17.26
Chapter Three
Ascetics and Brahmins (2nd)
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: “Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā lābhasakkārasilokassa samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṁ nappajānanti …pe…
segs.e: “There are ascetics and brahmins who don’t truly understand the origin, disappearance, gratification, drawback, and escape when it comes to possessions, honor, and popularity …
There are ascetics and brahmins who do truly understand …”
Linked Discourses 17.27
Chapter Three
Ascetics and Brahmins (3rd)
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: “Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā lābhasakkārasilokaṁ yathābhūtaṁ nappajānanti, lābhasakkārasilokasamudayaṁ nappajānanti, lābhasakkārasilokanirodhaṁ nappajānanti, lābhasakkārasilokanirodhagāminiṁ paṭipadaṁ nappajānanti …pe…
segs.e: “There are ascetics and brahmins who don’t truly understand possessions, honor, and popularity, their origin, their cessation, and the path that leads to their cessation …
There are ascetics and brahmins who do truly understand …”
Linked Discourses 17.28
Chapter Three
Skin
At Sāvatthī.
“Possessions, honor, and popularity are grim …

segs.p: Lābhasakkārasiloko, bhikkhave, chaviṁ chindati, chaviṁ chetvā cammaṁ chindati, cammaṁ chetvā maṁsaṁ chindati, maṁsaṁ chetvā nhāruṁ chindati, nhāruṁ chetvā aṭṭhiṁ chindati, aṭṭhiṁ chetvā aṭṭhimiñjaṁ āhacca tiṭṭhati.
segs.e: They cut through the outer skin, the inner skin, the flesh, sinews, and bones, until they reach the marrow and keep pressing.
So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”
Linked Discourses 17.29
Chapter Three
A Rope
At Sāvatthī.
“Possessions, honor, and popularity are grim …

segs.p: Lābhasakkārasiloko, bhikkhave, chaviṁ chindati, chaviṁ chetvā cammaṁ chindati, cammaṁ chetvā maṁsaṁ chindati, maṁsaṁ chetvā nhāruṁ chindati, nhāruṁ chetvā aṭṭhiṁ chindati, aṭṭhiṁ chetvā aṭṭhimiñjaṁ āhacca tiṭṭhati.
segs.e: They cut through the outer skin, the inner skin, the flesh, sinews, and bones, until they reach the marrow and keep pressing.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, balavā puriso daḷhāya vāḷarajjuyā jaṅghaṁ veṭhetvā ghaṁseyya.
segs.e: Suppose a strong man was to twist a strong horse-hair rope around your shin and tighten it.

segs.p: Sā chaviṁ chindeyya, chaviṁ chetvā cammaṁ chindeyya, cammaṁ chetvā maṁsaṁ chindeyya, maṁsaṁ chetvā nhāruṁ chindeyya, nhāruṁ chetvā aṭṭhiṁ chindeyya, aṭṭhiṁ chetvā aṭṭhimiñjaṁ āhacca tiṭṭheyya.
segs.e: It would cut through the outer skin, the inner skin, the flesh, sinews, and bones, until it reached the marrow and kept pressing.

segs.p: Evameva kho, bhikkhave, lābhasakkārasiloko chaviṁ chindati, chaviṁ chetvā cammaṁ chindati, cammaṁ chetvā maṁsaṁ chindati, maṁsaṁ chetvā nhāruṁ chindati, nhāruṁ chetvā aṭṭhiṁ chindati, aṭṭhiṁ chetvā aṭṭhimiñjaṁ āhacca tiṭṭhati.
segs.e: In the same way, possessions, honor, and popularity cut through the outer skin, the inner skin, the flesh, sinews, and bones, until they reach the marrow and keep pressing.
So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”
Linked Discourses 17.30
Chapter Three
A Mendicant With Defilements Ended
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: “Yopi so, bhikkhave, bhikkhu arahaṁ khīṇāsavo tassapāhaṁ lābhasakkārasiloko antarāyāya vadāmī”ti.
segs.e: “Mendicants, possessions, honor, and popularity are an obstacle even for a mendicant who is perfected, with defilements ended.”

segs.p: Evaṁ vutte, āyasmā ānando bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: When he said this, Venerable Ānanda said to the Buddha,

segs.p: “kissa pana, bhante, khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno lābhasakkārasiloko antarāyāyā”ti?
segs.e: “Sir, what do possessions, honor, and popularity obstruct for a mendicant with defilements ended?”

segs.p: “Yā hissa sā, ānanda, akuppā cetovimutti nāhaṁ tassā lābhasakkārasilokaṁ antarāyāya vadāmi.
segs.e: “Ānanda, I don’t say that possessions, honor, and popularity obstruct the unshakable freedom of heart.

segs.p: Ye ca khvassa, ānanda, appamattassa ātāpino pahitattassa viharato diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārā adhigatā tesāhamassa lābhasakkārasilokaṁ antarāyāya vadāmi.
segs.e: But I do say that possessions, honor, and popularity obstruct the achievement of blissful meditations in this life for a meditator who is diligent, keen, and resolute.

segs.p: Evaṁ dāruṇo kho, ānanda, lābhasakkārasiloko kaṭuko pharuso antarāyiko anuttarassa yogakkhemassa adhigamāya.
segs.e: So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity—bitter and harsh, an obstacle to reaching the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.
So you should train like this:

segs.p: ‘uppannaṁ lābhasakkārasilokaṁ pajahissāma, na ca no uppanno lābhasakkārasiloko cittaṁ pariyādāya ṭhassatī’ti.
segs.e: ‘We will give up arisen possessions, honor, and popularity, and we won’t let them occupy our minds.’
That’s how you should train.”
Linked Discourses 17.31
Chapter Four
Schism
At Sāvatthī.
“Possessions, honor, and popularity are grim …

segs.p: Lābhasakkārasilokena abhibhūto pariyādiṇṇacitto, bhikkhave, devadatto saṅghaṁ bhindi.
segs.e: Devadatta split the Saṅgha because his mind was overcome and overwhelmed by possessions, honor, and popularity.
So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”
Linked Discourses 17.32
Chapter Four
Skillful Root
At Sāvatthī.
“Possessions, honor, and popularity are grim …

segs.p: Lābhasakkārasilokena abhibhūtassa pariyādiṇṇacittassa, bhikkhave, devadattassa kusalamūlaṁ samucchedamagamā.
segs.e: Devadatta cut off his skillful root because his mind was overcome and overwhelmed by possessions, honor, and popularity.
So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”
Linked Discourses 17.33
Chapter Four
Skillful Quality
At Sāvatthī.
“Possessions, honor, and popularity are grim …

segs.p: Lābhasakkārasilokena abhibhūtassa pariyādiṇṇacittassa, bhikkhave, devadattassa kusalo dhammo samucchedamagamā.
segs.e: Devadatta cut off his skillful quality because his mind was overcome and overwhelmed by possessions, honor, and popularity.
So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”
Linked Discourses 17.34
Chapter Four
Bright Quality
At Sāvatthī.
“Possessions, honor, and popularity are grim …

segs.p: Lābhasakkārasilokena abhibhūtassa pariyādiṇṇacittassa, bhikkhave, devadattassa sukko dhammo samucchedamagamā.
segs.e: Devadatta cut off his bright quality because his mind was overcome and overwhelmed by possessions, honor, and popularity.
So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”
Linked Discourses 17.35
Chapter Four
Shortly After He Left

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā rājagahe viharati gijjhakūṭe pabbate acirapakkante devadatte.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain, not long after Devadatta had left.

segs.p: Tatra kho bhagavā devadattaṁ ārabbha bhikkhū āmantesi:
segs.e: There the Buddha spoke to the mendicants about Devadatta:

segs.p: “attavadhāya, bhikkhave, devadattassa lābhasakkārasiloko udapādi, parābhavāya devadattassa lābhasakkārasiloko udapādi.
segs.e: “Possessions, honor, and popularity came to Devadatta for his own ruin and downfall.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, kadalī attavadhāya phalaṁ deti, parābhavāya phalaṁ deti;
segs.e: It’s like a banana plant …

segs.p: evameva kho, bhikkhave, attavadhāya devadattassa lābhasakkārasiloko udapādi, parābhavāya devadattassa lābhasakkārasiloko udapādi.
Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, veḷu attavadhāya phalaṁ deti, parābhavāya phalaṁ deti;
segs.e: or a bamboo …

segs.p: evameva kho, bhikkhave, attavadhāya devadattassa lābhasakkārasiloko udapādi, parābhavāya devadattassa lābhasakkārasiloko udapādi.
Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, naḷo attavadhāya phalaṁ deti, parābhavāya phalaṁ deti;
segs.e: or a reed, all of which bear fruit to their own ruin and downfall …

segs.p: evameva kho, bhikkhave, attavadhāya devadattassa lābhasakkārasiloko udapādi, parābhavāya devadattassa lābhasakkārasiloko udapādi.
Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, assatarī attavadhāya gabbhaṁ gaṇhāti, parābhavāya gabbhaṁ gaṇhāti;
segs.e: It’s like a mule, which becomes pregnant to its own ruin and downfall.

segs.p: evameva kho, bhikkhave, attavadhāya devadattassa lābhasakkārasiloko udapādi, parābhavāya devadattassa lābhasakkārasiloko udapādi.
segs.e: In the same way, possessions, honor, and popularity came to Devadatta for his own ruin and downfall.
So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity.
That’s how you should train.”
That is what the Buddha said.

segs.p: Idaṁ vatvāna sugato athāparaṁ etadavoca satthā:
segs.e: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:
“The banana plant is destroyed by its own fruit,
as are the bamboo and the reed.
Honor destroys a reprobate,
as pregnancy destroys a mule.”
Linked Discourses 17.36
Chapter Four
Five Hundred Carts
Near Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena devadattassa ajātasattukumāro pañcahi rathasatehi sāyaṁ pātaṁ upaṭṭhānaṁ gacchati, pañca ca thālipākasatāni bhattābhihāro abhiharīyati.
segs.e: Now at that time Prince Ajātasattu was going with five hundred carts at daybreak and dusk to attend on Devadatta, presenting him with an offering of five hundred servings of food.

segs.p: Atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṁsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdiṁsu. Ekamantaṁ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū bhagavantaṁ etadavocuṁ:
segs.e: Then several mendicants went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

segs.p: “devadattassa, bhante, ajātasattukumāro pañcahi rathasatehi sāyaṁ pātaṁ upaṭṭhānaṁ gacchati, pañca ca thālipākasatāni bhattābhihāro abhiharīyatī”ti.
segs.e: “Sir, Prince Ajātasattu is going with five hundred carts at daybreak and dusk to attend on Devadatta, presenting him with an offering of five hundred servings of food.”
“Mendicants, don’t envy Devadatta’s possessions, honor, and popularity.

segs.p: Yāvakīvañca, bhikkhave, devadattassa ajātasattukumāro pañcahi rathasatehi sāyaṁ pātaṁ upaṭṭhānaṁ gamissati, pañca ca thālipākasatāni bhattābhihāro āharīyissati, hāniyeva, bhikkhave, devadattassa pāṭikaṅkhā kusalesu dhammesu, no vuddhi.
segs.e: As long as Prince Ajātasattu goes with five hundred carts at daybreak and dusk to attend on Devadatta, presenting him with an offering of five hundred servings of food, Devadatta can expect decline, not growth, in skillful qualities.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, caṇḍassa kukkurassa nāsāya pittaṁ bhindeyyuṁ, evañhi so, bhikkhave, kukkuro bhiyyoso mattāya caṇḍataro assa;
segs.e: If they were to lance a boil on a wild dog’s nose, it would get even wilder.

segs.p: evameva, bhikkhave, yāvakīvañca devadattassa ajātasattukumāro pañcahi rathasatehi sāyaṁ pātaṁ upaṭṭhānaṁ gamissati, pañca ca thālipākasatāni bhattābhihāro āharīyissati, hāniyeva, bhikkhave, devadattassa pāṭikaṅkhā kusalesu dhammesu, no vuddhi.
segs.e: In the same way, as long as Prince Ajātasattu goes with five hundred carts at daybreak and dusk to attend on Devadatta, presenting him with an offering of five hundred servings of food, Devadatta can expect decline, not growth, in skillful qualities.
So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”
Linked Discourses 17.37
Chapter Four
Mother
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: “Dāruṇo, bhikkhave, lābhasakkārasiloko kaṭuko pharuso antarāyiko anuttarassa yogakkhemassa adhigamāya.
segs.e: “Possessions, honor, and popularity are grim, bitter, and harsh. They’re an obstacle to reaching the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.

segs.p: Idhāhaṁ, bhikkhave, ekaccaṁ puggalaṁ evaṁ cetasā ceto paricca pajānāmi:
segs.e: When I’ve comprehended the mind of a certain individual, I understand:
‘This venerable would not tell a deliberate lie even for the sake of their mother.’

segs.p: Tamenaṁ passāmi aparena samayena lābhasakkārasilokena abhibhūtaṁ pariyādiṇṇacittaṁ sampajānamusā bhāsantaṁ.
segs.e: But some time later I see them tell a deliberate lie because their mind is overcome and overwhelmed by possessions, honor, and popularity.

segs.p: Evaṁ dāruṇo kho, bhikkhave, lābhasakkārasiloko kaṭuko pharuso antarāyiko anuttarassa yogakkhemassa adhigamāya.
segs.e: So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity—bitter and harsh, an obstacle to reaching the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.
So you should train like this:
‘We will give up arisen possessions, honor, and popularity, and we won’t let them occupy our minds.’

segs.p: Na ca no uppanno lābhasakkārasiloko cittaṁ pariyādāya ṭhassatī’ti.

segs.e: That’s how you should train.”
Linked Discourses 17.38–43

At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: “Dāruṇo, bhikkhave, lābhasakkārasiloko kaṭuko pharuso antarāyiko anuttarassa yogakkhemassa adhigamāya.
segs.e: “Possessions, honor, and popularity are grim, bitter, and harsh. They’re an obstacle to reaching the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.

segs.p: Idhāhaṁ, bhikkhave, ekaccaṁ puggalaṁ evaṁ cetasā ceto paricca pajānāmi:
segs.e: When I’ve comprehended the mind of a certain individual, I understand:
‘This venerable would not tell a deliberate lie even for the sake of their father.’ …”

“‘… brother.’ …”
“‘… sister.’ …”
“‘… daughter.’ …”
“‘… wife.’

segs.p: Tamenaṁ passāmi aparena samayena lābhasakkārasilokena abhibhūtaṁ pariyādiṇṇacittaṁ sampajānamusā bhāsantaṁ.
segs.e: But some time later I see them tell a deliberate lie because their mind is overcome and overwhelmed by possessions, honor, and popularity.

segs.p: Evaṁ dāruṇo kho, bhikkhave, lābhasakkārasiloko kaṭuko pharuso antarāyiko anuttarassa yogakkhemassa adhigamāya.
segs.e: So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity—bitter and harsh, an obstacle to reaching the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.
So you should train like this:

segs.p: ‘uppannaṁ lābhasakkārasilokaṁ pajahissāma, na ca no uppanno lābhasakkārasiloko cittaṁ pariyādāya ṭhassatī’ti.
segs.e: ‘We will give up arisen possessions, honor, and popularity, and we won’t let them occupy our minds.’
That’s how you should train.”
The Linked Discourses on possessions, honor, and popularity are complete.
